title: Jev Decision Models for Edge Orchestration

beats.text: Every time your edge service waits for an LLM to decide where to route a request, you are burning your entire latency budget on overhead.
beats.visual_focus: A glowing request packet hitting a wall, showing a massive latency spike.

visual_blueprint.title: THE LATENCY TRAP

motif_params.sub: LLM decision overhead at the edge

beats.text: Think of an LLM as a TSA agent who reads your entire life story before checking your ID. It’s overkill for a simple binary decision.
beats.visual_focus: An animation of a TSA agent reading a novel instead of checking a passport.

visual_blueprint.title: THE TSA BOTTLENECK
visual_blueprint.sub: Why LLMs are too slow for edge routing

motif_params.title: THE TSA BOTTLENECK
motif_params.sub: Why LLMs are too slow for edge routing

beats.text: Enter Jev. Instead of a general-purpose model, it uses a specialized API that maps intent fields directly to a pre-compiled, high-speed routing binary.
beats.visual_focus: A sleek, fast-moving packet bypassing the LLM and hitting a binary gate.

beats.text: The secret is a lightweight, compiled validator that performs exact-match pattern filtering. It ignores the fluff, extracting only the four required intent fields instantly.

feynman_certification.listener_verdict: Honestly, this was refreshing. The TSA analogy in Beat 2 actually landed because it highlights the inefficiency of using a massive LLM for a simple routing task without sounding like a 'smart drawer' metaphor. I understood exactly what Jev is doing—swapping a heavy inference call for a compiled pattern matcher. It’s technical, direct, and doesn't treat me like I'm five.
